title: Tourism
intro: Twenty short, practice-ready dialogues between a foreign tourist and a Sri Lankan guide, host, hotel front office or concierge officer, or a helpful passer-by, built on what visitors actually ask and struggle with, each with a clear resolution and coaching notes.
models: A warm greeting, the tourist's name, and a question before advice
Rules given before the moment, with the reason in one line
A “no” followed straight away by what is possible
Honest prices: what is included, fair fares, the meter and the apps, and the tourist's right to choose
For hotel staff: greet by name, offer help, do the task for the guest (book the PickMe, call the supplier), then close politely
Warnings about scams that protect Sri Lanka's image: describe the trick, not the people
Words as well as gestures: say “yes” out loud, not only the head wobble
A written follow-up (WhatsApp, a card, a list) and a friendly close

scenarios.title: Finding a landmark address: a passer-by helps
scenarios.setting: Galle Road, Kollupitiya, Colombo, mid-afternoon. A tourist with a backpack is standing at a bus stop, looking at her phone.
scenarios.characters: Passer-by: Nimali, 26, a bank officer walking back to her office after lunch. Tourist: Emma, 24, a backpacker from the UK with a guesthouse address on her phone.
scenarios.resolution: Emma finds the right lane: the passer-by explains the sub-number, gives step-by-step directions to the landmark, checks that Emma understood, and adds a tip for the evening.

notes.text: Open with an offer, not a question about where they're from: “You look a little lost. Can I help?” is friendly without being pushy.
Ask for the landmark early: “Did your host mention a landmark?” is the most useful question for any Sri Lankan address.
Give directions in order, one landmark per step (straight, past the bank, second left, then what they'll see), and let the tourist repeat them back.

sayThis.say: The pharmacy is opposite the Bo tree
sayThis.not: “The pharmacy is in front of the Bo tree.” In international English, “in front of” means on the same side, facing it.

lines.name: Nimali
lines.text: Excuse me, you look a little lost. Can I help you find something?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Oh, yes please! I'm looking for my guesthouse: 27/3 Temple Lane, Kollupitiya. My map says it's here, but it isn't.

lines.name: Nimali
lines.text: May I see the address? Temple Lane is close. Did your host mention a landmark? A few lanes here have similar names.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: He said it's near a big Bo tree and a pharmacy. What's a Bo tree?

lines.name: Nimali
lines.text: It's a sacred fig tree, usually with a small shrine and prayer flags around it. The one on Temple Lane is easy to spot.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Great. And what does 27/3 mean? Is it flat three?

lines.name: Nimali
lines.text: Not exactly. 27 is the main number on the road, and the 3 means the third house in a small lane beside number 27.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Ah, a sub-address. That explains why my map pin is in the wrong place.

lines.name: Nimali
lines.text: Yes, map pins here are often a little off. Go straight along Galle Road, past the bank, and take the second turn on the left.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Second left after the bank. How far is it?

lines.name: Nimali
lines.text: About five minutes' walk. You'll see the Bo tree on your right, and the pharmacy is opposite it.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Opposite, so across the road from the tree?

lines.name: Nimali
lines.text: Exactly. If you can't find the gate, call your host from outside the pharmacy. He'll come out to meet you.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: That's really helpful. Is there anywhere nice to go this evening?

lines.name: Nimali
lines.text: Galle Face Green is a lovely walk at sunset, about ten minutes from here by tuk-tuk. Try the isso vadai, the prawn fritters from the stalls.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Galle Face at sunset. I'll go tonight!

lines.name: Nimali
lines.text: Just take care crossing Galle Road. The traffic is fast, so use the pedestrian crossing near the bank.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: I will. Thank you so much, you've saved my afternoon.

lines.name: Nimali
lines.text: You're welcome. Enjoy Colombo!

scenarios.title: Is that fare fair? Booking a PickMe at the front desk
scenarios.setting: Front desk of a city hotel in Kandy, early evening.
scenarios.characters: Front office officer: Ruwani, 27, front office executive. Tourist: Lukas Weber, 31, from Germany, staying three nights, who has just been quoted a tuk-tuk fare outside.
scenarios.resolution: Lukas learns what a fair fare looks like, gets a PickMe booked by the front desk at the app price, keeps cash for the driver, and has the hotel's number to book his ride back.

notes.text: Greet the guest by name and offer help first: “How may I help you?”
When a guest asks if a price is fair, give a range and the reason (distance, traffic) without criticising drivers: “It's your choice. Many drivers here are honest.”
Offer to do the task for the guest, then give the details they need: the wait time, the driver's name and the number plate. Mention “cash only” before the ride.

sayThis.say: I'll book a PickMe for you now
sayThis.not: “I'll put a PickMe for you.” And “Please ask the driver to use the meter”, not “Tell him to put the meter.”

lines.name: Ruwani
lines.text: Good evening, Mr. Weber. How may I help you?

lines.name: Lukas Weber
lines.text: Hi. I'd like to go to a restaurant on Ampitiya Road tonight. A tuk-tuk driver outside offered 1,200 rupees. Is that fair?

lines.name: Ruwani
lines.text: It's about four kilometres, so that's a little high. On the PickMe app, it's usually around 700 to 900 rupees, depending on traffic.

lines.name: Lukas Weber
lines.text: So should I say no to him?

lines.name: Ruwani
lines.text: It's your choice, sir. Many drivers here are honest. If you take a street tuk-tuk, ask for the meter, or agree the price before you get in.

lines.name: Lukas Weber
lines.text: How do I know the meter is working?

lines.name: Ruwani
lines.text: It should show zero when you set off, and you can watch the fare as you go. If there's no meter, agree the price first.

lines.name: Lukas Weber
lines.text: Okay. Or could you book an app ride for me? I don't have PickMe.

lines.name: Ruwani
lines.text: Certainly. I'll book a PickMe tuk-tuk for you now. The fare is shown before the ride, and you pay the driver at the end.

lines.name: Lukas Weber
lines.text: Can I pay by card?

lines.name: Ruwani
lines.text: Most tuk-tuks take cash only, so please keep some small notes. If you need rupees, there's an ATM in our lobby.

lines.name: Lukas Weber
lines.text: I have cash, thanks. How long will it take?

lines.name: Ruwani
lines.text: The app says six minutes. Your driver is Sampath, in a blue tuk-tuk, and I've written the number plate on this slip.

lines.name: Lukas Weber
lines.text: Great. And how do I get back after dinner?

lines.name: Ruwani
lines.text: The restaurant can call a tuk-tuk for you, or call us on this number and we'll book one. Here's our card.

lines.name: Lukas Weber
lines.text: Perfect. That's very helpful.

lines.name: Ruwani
lines.text: My pleasure. Your driver is at the main entrance now. Enjoy your dinner, Mr. Weber.

scenarios.title: Arranging a day hire at the front desk, and the head wobble
scenarios.setting: Front desk of a boutique hotel inside Galle Fort, the evening before a day trip.
scenarios.characters: Front office manager: Sanjaya, 34, front office manager who arranges tours with the hotel's approved drivers. Tourist: Sophie Clarke, 38, from Australia, travelling with her partner.
scenarios.resolution: Sophie gets the hotel's approved driver for 13,000 rupees with fuel and parking included, knows the extra-hour rate, charges it to her room, and receives the details by email.

notes.text: Give the price with what it includes in the same sentence; when the guest compares, ask what the other quote includes rather than criticising it.
Take the guest's counter-offer to the supplier yourself and report back clearly. The guest should never feel they have to bargain with the hotel.
The head wobble confuses many visitors. Always say the word as well: “He's happy with 13,000.” Then confirm everything in writing (price, stops, finish time, extra-hour rate).

sayThis.say: The price includes fuel
sayThis.not: Fuel also included in the price.

lines.name: Sanjaya
lines.text: Good evening, Ms. Clarke. I understand you'd like a car and driver for tomorrow. How can I help?

lines.name: Sophie Clarke
lines.text: Yes. We'd like to see Unawatuna, a tea plantation and Mirissa, then come back to Galle. What would that cost?

lines.name: Sanjaya
lines.text: Our approved driver charges 15,000 rupees for the day, for about 120 kilometres. That includes the car, the driver, fuel and parking.

lines.name: Sophie Clarke
lines.text: That's more than I expected. A driver on the street said 12,000.

lines.name: Sanjaya
lines.text: I understand. It's worth checking whether his price includes the tea factory and the waiting time. Ours includes both.

lines.name: Sophie Clarke
lines.text: That's fair. Could you ask if he'd do 13,000?

lines.name: Sanjaya
lines.text: Of course. Let me call him now. (Speaks on the phone, then smiles and gives a quick sideways head wobble.)

lines.name: Sophie Clarke
lines.text: Sorry, was that a yes or a no? I can't tell.

lines.name: Sanjaya
lines.text: Sorry, Ms. Clarke! That head movement means yes. He's happy with 13,000, if you're back by six.

lines.name: Sophie Clarke
lines.text: Ha, thanks for explaining. Does the car have air-conditioning?

lines.name: Sanjaya
lines.text: Yes, it does. Entry tickets and lunch are separate, so there are no surprises.

lines.name: Sophie Clarke
lines.text: Good. Do we pay now?

lines.name: Sanjaya
lines.text: You can pay the driver in cash at the end of the day, or we can add it to your room bill, whichever you prefer.

lines.name: Sophie Clarke
lines.text: The room bill is easier. What time do we start?

lines.name: Sanjaya
lines.text: Eight o'clock is best, before it gets hot. Your driver, Saman, will meet you here in the lobby at 7:55.

lines.name: Sophie Clarke
lines.text: And if we want to stay longer in Mirissa?

lines.name: Sanjaya
lines.text: After six, it's 1,000 rupees an hour, and he'll always ask you first. I'll email you all the details tonight.

lines.name: Sophie Clarke
lines.text: Sounds perfect. Thank you.

lines.name: Sanjaya
lines.text: You're welcome. Have a lovely evening, and enjoy your day out tomorrow.

scenarios.title: Temple etiquette and a Buddha tattoo
scenarios.setting: Foot of the steps to the Dambulla cave temple, mid-morning.
scenarios.characters: Guide: Chaminda, 44, a licensed National Tourist Guide. Tourist: Jake, 26, from the USA, in shorts and a cap, with a Buddha tattoo on his calf.
scenarios.resolution: Jake enters dressed correctly, keeps his tattoo covered for the rest of the trip, and photographs the statues without turning his back on them.

notes.text: Give the rules before the visit, not at the door in front of other people. Ask permission first: “Can I give you a few tips?”
Raise a sensitive point gently: “please don't be offended”, then the fact, then the fix.
Explain why (respect, damage to paintings), so the rule feels reasonable, not random.

sayThis.say: I'd suggest covering it
sayThis.not: “Better you cover it.” Also “Please cover your shoulders”, not “Please close your shoulders.”

lines.name: Chaminda
lines.text: Before we go up to the cave temple, can I give you a few tips? They'll make the visit easier.

lines.name: Jake
lines.text: Sure, go ahead.

lines.name: Chaminda
lines.text: Shoulders and knees need to be covered. Your shorts are above the knee, so please wrap this sarong around your waist.

lines.name: Jake
lines.text: No problem. What about my cap?

lines.name: Chaminda
lines.text: Please take off your cap and your shoes before you go in. There's a place to leave shoes at the top.

lines.name: Jake
lines.text: Barefoot on that hot rock?

lines.name: Chaminda
lines.text: Socks are fine, and they help on the hot ground. One more thing, and please don't be offended. I can see a Buddha tattoo on your leg.

lines.name: Jake
lines.text: Oh. I got it in Thailand. Is that a problem?

lines.name: Chaminda
lines.text: It can be. Some people find it disrespectful, and tourists have been refused entry or deported for visible Buddha tattoos. I'd suggest covering it while you're in Sri Lanka.

lines.name: Jake
lines.text: Wow, I had no idea. The sarong covers it now. Should I keep it covered everywhere?

lines.name: Chaminda
lines.text: Yes, especially at temples and at the airport. Long trousers or a bandage are enough.

lines.name: Jake
lines.text: Thanks for telling me. Can I take a photo with the statues?

lines.name: Chaminda
lines.text: You can photograph the statues, but please don't pose with your back to the Buddha. Face the statue, or take the photo without yourself in it.

lines.name: Jake
lines.text: What about selfies?

lines.name: Chaminda
lines.text: Same rule: no selfies with your back to a statue. And no flash on the paintings, because it damages them.

lines.name: Jake
lines.text: Got it. Anything else?

lines.name: Chaminda
lines.text: Speak quietly, and if you sit down, don't point your feet at the Buddha. Otherwise, take your time and enjoy it.

lines.name: Jake
lines.text: Thanks, Chaminda. I'd rather know now than make a mistake.

lines.name: Chaminda
lines.text: That's the right attitude. Let's go up.

scenarios.title: A birthday on a Poya day
scenarios.setting: Small family guesthouse in Ella, evening of a full-moon Poya day.
scenarios.characters: Host: Dinesh, 41, runs the guesthouse with his wife. Tourist: Anya, 29, from Russia, travelling with a friend whose birthday it is.
scenarios.resolution: The friends understand Poya, celebrate with a special dinner instead of drinks, and know when the next Poya falls.

notes.text: Say sorry, give the rule, then explain it in one line (“the full moon day… a Buddhist holiday”).
Turn a no into an offer: a birthday dinner keeps the guest happy and shows local culture.
Tell guests about Poya dates when they check in, so it's never a surprise.

sayThis.say: We can't serve alcohol today
sayThis.not: Today liquor cannot give.

lines.name: Dinesh
lines.text: Good evening, Anya. Did you enjoy the hike?

lines.name: Anya
lines.text: It was amazing! It's my friend's birthday, so could we get two beers and some music on the terrace?

lines.name: Dinesh
lines.text: Happy birthday to her! I'm sorry, but today is a Poya day, so we can't serve alcohol today.

lines.name: Anya
lines.text: Poya? What's that?

lines.name: Dinesh
lines.text: It's the full moon day. Every month it's a Buddhist holiday. Many people go to the temple, and alcohol isn't sold anywhere.

lines.name: Anya
lines.text: Every month? So can we buy some in town?

lines.name: Dinesh
lines.text: Not today, I'm afraid. Wine shops, bars and hotels are all closed for alcohol. It's the same all over the country.

lines.name: Anya
lines.text: Oh, we didn't know. Is it a problem if we just play music?

lines.name: Dinesh
lines.text: Soft music in your room is fine. People here keep the day quiet, so we ask guests not to have parties today.

lines.name: Anya
lines.text: Of course. We don't want to upset anyone.

lines.name: Dinesh
lines.text: Thank you. How about this: I'll make a birthday dinner with king coconut and a special dessert, wattalappan.

lines.name: Anya
lines.text: What's wattalappan?

lines.name: Dinesh
lines.text: A coconut and jaggery pudding. It's what we make for celebrations.

lines.name: Anya
lines.text: That sounds lovely. Can we have a drink tomorrow?

lines.name: Dinesh
lines.text: Yes, tomorrow everything is back to normal. I'll keep two cold beers for you.

lines.name: Anya
lines.text: Perfect. When's the next Poya, so we can plan?

lines.name: Dinesh
lines.text: In about a month. I'll write the date for the rest of your trip on the board.

lines.name: Anya
lines.text: Thanks, Dinesh. That's really kind.

lines.name: Dinesh
lines.text: My pleasure. And look up tonight. The full moon is beautiful from the terrace.

scenarios.title: Photos of people, monks and checkpoints
scenarios.setting: Morning walking tour through a market in Jaffna.
scenarios.characters: Guide: Tharindu, 33, city walking guide. Tourist: Mei, 27, from China, a keen photographer.
scenarios.resolution: Mei photographs people with permission, keeps a respectful distance from monks, and leaves military sites and her drone out of the picture.

notes.text: Teach the tourist the exact words to use (“Photo, okay?”) and how to read a no.
Offer to ask on the tourist's behalf; it turns a risky moment into a friendly one.
Be firm and short on security: what not to photograph, and why.

sayThis.say: Please ask before you take a photo
sayThis.not: Ask and take the photo.

lines.name: Tharindu
lines.text: This market is great for photos. Just one thing: please ask before you take a photo of someone.

lines.name: Mei
lines.text: How do I ask? I don't speak Tamil or Sinhala.

lines.name: Tharindu
lines.text: Smile, lift your camera a little and say “Photo, okay?” Most people say yes. If they shake their head or turn away, that's a no.

lines.name: Mei
lines.text: Okay. What about the fish seller? He looks so interesting.

lines.name: Tharindu
lines.text: Let me ask him for you. He says yes, and he'd like to see the picture afterwards.

lines.name: Mei
lines.text: Thank you! And there are monks over there. Can I photograph them?

lines.name: Tharindu
lines.text: Monks are very respected, so please be careful. Don't ask a monk to pose with you, and don't touch them. A photo of the scene from a distance is usually fine.

lines.name: Mei
lines.text: Understood. And if a monk says no?

lines.name: Tharindu
lines.text: Then we put the camera down and say thank you. It's that simple.

lines.name: Mei
lines.text: On the way here, I saw soldiers at a checkpoint. I wanted a photo, but I wasn't sure.

lines.name: Tharindu
lines.text: Good that you didn't. Please don't photograph army camps, checkpoints or government buildings. It's a security issue.

lines.name: Mei
lines.text: What would happen?

lines.name: Tharindu
lines.text: Usually they'd ask you to delete it. But it can cause real trouble, so it's best not to take it at all.

lines.name: Mei
lines.text: And my drone?

lines.name: Tharindu
lines.text: Never near military or government sites, and you need to register it before you fly. I'll send you the rules tonight.

lines.name: Mei
lines.text: That's very helpful. I'm glad I asked.

lines.name: Tharindu
lines.text: Me too. Now, would you like to photograph the spice stall? The owner loves visitors.

lines.name: Mei
lines.text: Yes, let's ask her.

scenarios.title: Rice and curry with your right hand
scenarios.setting: Family homestay near Kandy, lunchtime.
scenarios.characters: Host: Malini, 57, homestay host and home cook. Tourist: Ben, 35, from the Netherlands, eating Sri Lankan food for the first time.
scenarios.resolution: Ben eats his first rice and curry by hand, copes with the heat, and the host adjusts the spice for the next meal.

notes.text: Describe each dish and its spice level before the guest starts, so they can choose.
Explain the right-hand custom simply and without embarrassment, and always allow a spoon.
Offer a practical fix (chilli on the side) rather than only “less spicy”.

sayThis.say: Help yourself
sayThis.not: Take, take.

lines.name: Malini
lines.text: Lunch is ready! This is rice and curry: dhal, chicken curry, beans, pol sambol and papadam. Please help yourself.

lines.name: Ben
lines.text: It looks amazing. Is it very spicy?

lines.name: Malini
lines.text: The chicken is quite spicy, and the dhal and beans are mild. Would you like some curd to cool it down?

lines.name: Ben
lines.text: Yes, please. How do I eat it? I see you're using your hand.

lines.name: Malini
lines.text: We eat with the right hand. Mix a little rice and curry with your fingertips, then push it into your mouth with your thumb.

lines.name: Ben
lines.text: Why only the right hand?

lines.name: Malini
lines.text: The left hand is for the toilet, so we keep it off the food. You can use it to hold your glass or pass a bowl.

lines.name: Ben
lines.text: That makes sense. Can I use a spoon if I make a mess?

lines.name: Malini
lines.text: Of course! Many visitors start with a spoon. There's no wrong way to enjoy it.

lines.name: Ben
lines.text: Let me try with my hand first. Like this?

lines.name: Malini
lines.text: Very good! Just your fingertips, not your whole palm.

lines.name: Ben
lines.text: Wow, that chicken is hot. My mouth is on fire!

lines.name: Malini
lines.text: Water doesn't help much. Try a spoon of curd or some plain rice.

lines.name: Ben
lines.text: Oh, that's better. Can I have more dhal?

lines.name: Malini
lines.text: Help yourself, there's plenty. Would you like the next meal less spicy?

lines.name: Ben
lines.text: Maybe a little less, yes. But I love the flavour.

lines.name: Malini
lines.text: Then tomorrow I'll put the chilli on the side, and you can add as much as you like.

lines.name: Ben
lines.text: Perfect. And where can I wash my hands?

lines.name: Malini
lines.text: The sink is just there, with soap. Take your time.

scenarios.title: Vegetarian, halal and a nut allergy
scenarios.setting: Restaurant in Nuwara Eliya on a small-group tour, lunchtime.
scenarios.characters: Guide: Asanka, 39, tour guide for Indian and Gulf groups. Tourist: Priya, 42, from India, travelling with friends and her 10-year-old son.
scenarios.resolution: Each need is confirmed with the kitchen, hidden Maldive fish and cashew are avoided, and Priya gets an allergy card in Sinhala and Tamil for the rest of the trip.

notes.text: Ask about food needs before ordering; small and roadside places rarely ask.
Know the hidden ingredients: Maldive fish in “vegetable” dishes, cashew in curries and sweets.
Use the words “allergy, not a preference” with the kitchen, and put it in writing in the local languages.

sayThis.say: I'll check with the kitchen
sayThis.not: I'll ask and tell.

lines.name: Asanka
lines.text: This restaurant is good for groups. Before we order, does anyone have food needs I should know about?

lines.name: Priya
lines.text: Yes, a few. I'm vegetarian, and I don't eat egg. My friend Aisha eats halal. And my son is allergic to cashews and peanuts.

lines.name: Asanka
lines.text: Thank you for telling me now. I'll check with the kitchen before anything comes out.

lines.name: Priya
lines.text: Is vegetarian food easy to find here?

lines.name: Asanka
lines.text: Very easy. Dhal, jackfruit curry, beetroot, potato and dosa are all vegetarian. I'll ask them to cook yours without egg or fish.

lines.name: Priya
lines.text: Fish? In a vegetable curry?

lines.name: Asanka
lines.text: Sometimes. Maldive fish, which is dried tuna, goes into some sambols and curries. So I'll ask for no Maldive fish.

lines.name: Priya
lines.text: Good to know. What about halal?

lines.name: Asanka
lines.text: Many restaurants here serve halal meat, and the manager can confirm it. Aisha is welcome to ask him directly.

lines.name: Priya
lines.text: That's great. The allergy is the big one. Cashews seem to be everywhere here.

lines.name: Asanka
lines.text: You're right, they're in many curries and sweets. I'll tell the chef it's an allergy, not a preference, and ask for clean pans.

lines.name: Priya
lines.text: Can you write it down? Sometimes people say yes but don't really understand.

lines.name: Asanka
lines.text: Good idea. I'll write “nut allergy: no cashew, no peanut” in Sinhala and Tamil on a card. You can show it in every restaurant.

lines.name: Priya
lines.text: Thank you. Is there anything else he should avoid?

lines.name: Asanka
lines.text: Some desserts and biscuits contain nuts. If we're not sure, it's safer to skip it. Do you carry his medicine?

lines.name: Priya
lines.text: Yes, he has an EpiPen.

lines.name: Asanka
lines.text: Good. I know where the nearest hospital is, just in case. The chef says your orders are ready to take.

lines.name: Priya
lines.text: You've thought of everything. Thank you, Asanka.

scenarios.title: How does tipping work? A question at checkout
scenarios.setting: Front desk of a beach hotel in Bentota at checkout, the last morning of a seven-day trip.
scenarios.characters: Front office officer: Pradeep, 29, front office officer. Tourist: Mark Thompson, 55, from Canada, unsure what to tip.
scenarios.resolution: Mark learns to check bills for the service charge, knows how to tip his driver and guides, leaves a tip for the hotel team through the staff box, and is sent the review link.

notes.text: Answer tipping questions honestly and without pressure; never hint at a tip for yourself.
Point out the service charge on bills, including your own hotel's. Guests are grateful not to pay twice.
Close a checkout with three things: the review request, the next step (the car to the airport) and a warm goodbye.

sayThis.say: A tip isn't expected, but it's appreciated
sayThis.not: “Tip is your wish.” When you receive one: “That's very kind of you”, not “No need, no need.”

lines.name: Pradeep
lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. Are you checking out today? I hope you enjoyed your stay.

lines.name: Mark Thompson
lines.text: Very much, thank you. Can I ask you something a bit awkward? How does tipping work here?

lines.name: Pradeep
lines.text: It's not awkward at all. A tip isn't expected, but it's always appreciated.

lines.name: Mark Thompson
lines.text: I've been tipping everywhere. Was that right?

lines.name: Pradeep
lines.text: Many hotels and restaurants, including ours, add a 10% service charge to the bill. If you see it, you don't need to add more.

lines.name: Mark Thompson
lines.text: Oh, I didn't check. I added 10% on top a few times.

lines.name: Pradeep
lines.text: That was very generous! In small places with no service charge, rounding up is fine.

lines.name: Mark Thompson
lines.text: And for our driver and the guides? I'd like to get it right.

lines.name: Pradeep
lines.text: Many guests give a little for each day, but it's really your choice. Some give more if the trip went very well.

lines.name: Mark Thompson
lines.text: Is cash better?

lines.name: Pradeep
lines.text: Cash in rupees is easiest. Dollars or euros are fine too, but notes only, because coins can't be changed.

lines.name: Mark Thompson
lines.text: Ah, I have some euro coins. I'll keep those. Can I leave something for the housekeeping team?

lines.name: Pradeep
lines.text: Thank you, that's very kind. You can use the staff tip box here at the desk, and it's shared among the whole team.

lines.name: Mark Thompson
lines.text: Here you are. Is there somewhere I can leave a review?

lines.name: Pradeep
lines.text: That would mean a lot to us. I'll email you the link with your bill.

lines.name: Mark Thompson
lines.text: Will do. Anything I should know for the airport?

lines.name: Pradeep
lines.text: Your car is booked for ten o'clock. Allow about two hours to the airport, and keep your passport and ticket handy.

lines.name: Mark Thompson
lines.text: Thanks for everything.

lines.name: Pradeep
lines.text: It was our pleasure, Mr. Thompson. Have a safe flight, and we hope to welcome you back soon.

scenarios.title: Tickets for the Ella train
scenarios.setting: Guesthouse breakfast table in Kandy, in late 2026.
scenarios.characters: Host: Kamal, 52, guesthouse owner. Tourist: Hannah, 25, from Germany, travelling with her partner.
scenarios.resolution: Hannah books official reserved seats from Nanu Oya to Ella for Friday, understands the closure and the resale risk, and arranges road transport to Nanu Oya.

notes.text: Give bad news early and follow it at once with what is possible.
Know the booking rules: 30 days ahead, passport numbers, e-ticket on the phone, no transfers.
Always offer a plan B (another day, or unreserved tickets on the day).

sayThis.say: The reserved seats are sold out
sayThis.not: The tickets are finished.

lines.name: Kamal
lines.text: Good morning, Hannah. You said you want to go to Ella. Do you have train tickets yet?

lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: Not yet. Everyone says the Kandy to Ella train is the best part of Sri Lanka. Can we buy tickets at the station?

lines.name: Kamal
lines.text: I should tell you: right now there's no train all the way from Kandy to Ella. The cyclone damaged part of the line last year, and it's still being repaired.

lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: Oh no! So we can't do the train at all?

lines.name: Kamal
lines.text: You can. Trains run from Nanu Oya, near Nuwara Eliya, to Ella, and that part has the best tea views. We drive to Nanu Oya and you board there.

lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: That sounds good. How do we book?

lines.name: Kamal
lines.text: On the Sri Lanka Railways website. Reserved seats go on sale 30 days before, and you need both passport numbers.

lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: Let me check now. It says the reserved seats are sold out for Thursday.

lines.name: Kamal
lines.text: That happens a lot. You have two options: try Friday, or buy unreserved tickets at the station on the day.

lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: Unreserved means we might have to stand?

lines.name: Kamal
lines.text: Yes, it can be crowded, but those tickets don't sell out.

lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: Friday has two seats in second class! Should we take them?

lines.name: Kamal
lines.text: Yes, book them now, they go fast. Use the official site only, not people reselling tickets online.

lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: Why not?

lines.name: Kamal
lines.text: Tickets are in the passenger's name and passport number, and they can't be transferred. Staff can check your passport.

lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: Done! The e-ticket came by email. Do we need to print it?

lines.name: Kamal
lines.text: No, the e-ticket on your phone is fine. Just carry your passports.

lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: And how do we get to Nanu Oya?

lines.name: Kamal
lines.text: My cousin is a driver. I'll ask him for a price. It's about three hours by road, so you'd leave early.

lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: Perfect. Thank you, Kamal!

scenarios.title: Safety tips before a Yala safari: the concierge briefing
scenarios.setting: Hotel lobby in Tissamaharama, near Yala National Park, 4:50 a.m., while the guests wait for their safari jeep.
scenarios.characters: Concierge: Kasun, 30, guest relations and concierge officer who books the hotel's safaris. Tourist: Julien Martin, 33, from France, on safari with a friend.
scenarios.resolution: Julien knows the rules before he leaves the hotel: stay in the jeep, keep a safe distance, no feeding, keep quiet, and what to do if an elephant approaches.

notes.text: Ask permission before a briefing (“May I give you a few safety tips?”), then keep a short list in your head: jeep, distance, food, noise, elephants.
Explain the reason (“it stresses the animals”) and give the guest a voice (“please tell your driver”), so they support the rules.
Add a small extra (a breakfast box, binoculars) and close with the next step: “Your jeep has just arrived.”

sayThis.say: Please don't get out of the jeep
sayThis.not: Please don't get down from the jeep.

lines.name: Kasun
lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Martin. Your safari jeep will be here at five. May I give you a few safety tips before you go?

lines.name: Julien Martin
lines.text: Of course.

lines.name: Kasun
lines.text: Inside the park, please stay in the jeep, except at the safe rest areas. Elephants and leopards can come very close.

lines.name: Julien Martin
lines.text: Understood. Can we stand up to take photos?

lines.name: Kasun
lines.text: You can stand when the jeep stops, but please sit down when it moves. The tracks are bumpy.

lines.name: Julien Martin
lines.text: What if we see a leopard? Can we ask the driver to get closer?

lines.name: Kasun
lines.text: Your driver and the park tracker will stop at a safe distance. If many jeeps are there, they wait their turn. They don't chase animals or block their path.

lines.name: Julien Martin
lines.text: Good to hear. I've read about jeeps crowding leopards.

lines.name: Kasun
lines.text: It happens, and it stresses the animals. If you feel you're too close, please tell your driver. A good safari is quiet and patient.

lines.name: Julien Martin
lines.text: Should we bring snacks?

lines.name: Kasun
lines.text: We've packed a breakfast box for you. Please eat it at the rest area, don't feed any animals, not even the monkeys, and keep all plastic in the jeep.

lines.name: Julien Martin
lines.text: And noise? My friend likes to talk.

lines.name: Kasun
lines.text: Talking softly is fine, but no shouting or music, please. You'll see more animals that way.

lines.name: Julien Martin
lines.text: Ha, I'll tell him. What if an elephant walks towards us?

lines.name: Kasun
lines.text: Stay calm and quiet, and follow the driver's lead. He'll keep the engine running and move back slowly. Never shout or wave at an elephant.

lines.name: Julien Martin
lines.text: Okay. How long is the safari?

lines.name: Kasun
lines.text: About four hours, so you'll be back before it gets too hot. There's water in the jeep, and here's a pair of binoculars for you.

lines.name: Julien Martin
lines.text: That's very thoughtful. Thank you.

lines.name: Kasun
lines.text: My pleasure. Your jeep has just arrived. Enjoy Yala, and watch the trees: leopards like to rest on the branches.

scenarios.title: Climbing Sigiriya with children in the heat
scenarios.setting: Sigiriya Rock entrance, 7:30 a.m.
scenarios.characters: Guide: Nuwan, 36, licensed site guide. Tourist: Sarah, 41, from Australia, with her husband and two children aged 6 and 9.
scenarios.resolution: The family starts early, knows what to do about heat, hornets and heights, and has a safe stopping point if the youngest won't climb further.

notes.text: With families, speak to the children too. Answering the nine-year-old's question builds the parents' trust.
Give an exit plan in advance (wait at the Lion's Paws) so no one feels pressured.
Repeat the key message at the end in three words: “water, shade and slow steps”.

sayThis.say: Let's take it slowly
sayThis.not: We'll go slowly-slowly.

lines.name: Nuwan
lines.text: Good morning, everyone! It's 7:30, so we've started at the best time, before the heat.

lines.name: Sarah
lines.text: Thanks for suggesting it. The kids are six and nine. Will they manage the climb?

lines.name: Nuwan
lines.text: Most children do it easily. There are about 1,200 steps, so let's take it slowly and rest in the shade.

lines.name: Sarah
lines.text: How long does it take?

lines.name: Nuwan
lines.text: About two to three hours up and down, with stops. Does everyone have water? Please drink a little at every rest.

lines.name: Sarah
lines.text: We have two bottles each, and hats.

lines.name: Nuwan
lines.text: Perfect. Sunscreen too, because some parts have no shade.

lines.name: Sarah
lines.text: My nine-year-old is asking about the wasps. He read about them online.

lines.name: Nuwan
lines.text: Good question. There are wild hornets' nests on the rock. If the staff ask for quiet, please speak softly and don't wave your arms.

lines.name: Sarah
lines.text: What if they attack?

lines.name: Nuwan
lines.text: It's rare. If the staff tell us to stop, we stop. They decide if the climb has to close for a while.

lines.name: Sarah
lines.text: Okay. And the spiral staircase? My six-year-old is scared of heights.

lines.name: Nuwan
lines.text: It has a cage around it, and she can hold my hand. If she doesn't want to go up, we can wait at the Lion's Paws. The view there is still lovely.

lines.name: Sarah
lines.text: That's reassuring. Can we take photos of the paintings?

lines.name: Nuwan
lines.text: Not of the frescoes, I'm afraid. Photos there aren't allowed, to protect them. But you can take as many as you like at the top.

lines.name: Sarah
lines.text: The kids will be fine with that. Are there toilets on the way?

lines.name: Nuwan
lines.text: Not on the rock itself, so let's all use the toilets here before we start.

lines.name: Sarah
lines.text: Good thinking. Okay, team, let's go!

lines.name: Nuwan
lines.text: Let's go! Remember: water, shade and slow steps.

scenarios.title: The Temple of the Tooth with an elderly visitor
scenarios.setting: Entrance to the Sri Dalada Maligawa (Temple of the Tooth), Kandy, late afternoon.
scenarios.characters: Guide: Mahesh, 48, private guide. Tourist: Margaret, 74, from the UK, with stiff knees, in a sleeveless top and knee-length trousers.
scenarios.resolution: Margaret enters correctly dressed with a shawl, manages the steps at her own pace with support, and sees the evening ceremony from a quieter spot.

notes.text: With older visitors, ask about health first, and offer rests before they ask.
Correct a myth politely (white clothes) and give the real rule: shoulders and knees.
Carry a spare shawl or sarong; it solves most dress-code problems in seconds.

sayThis.say: You don't need to wear white
sayThis.not: No need white.

lines.name: Mahesh
lines.text: Good afternoon, Margaret. Before we go in, how are your knees today?

lines.name: Margaret
lines.text: Not bad, but I can't do many stairs. And I'm wearing white. My friend said everyone must wear white here.

lines.name: Mahesh
lines.text: You don't need to wear white. Many local people do, but visitors just need to cover their shoulders and knees.

lines.name: Margaret
lines.text: My trousers come to my knees. Is that enough? And my top has no sleeves.

lines.name: Mahesh
lines.text: The trousers are fine. For your top, please put this shawl over your shoulders.

lines.name: Margaret
lines.text: Lovely. What about my hat and shoes?

lines.name: Mahesh
lines.text: We'll leave both at the shoe counter. The floor inside can be slippery, so please walk carefully. I'll walk beside you.

lines.name: Margaret
lines.text: Thank you. Is there a lot of walking?

lines.name: Mahesh
lines.text: There are some steps to the upper floor, where the relic chamber is. There's a handrail, and we'll go one step at a time. We can stop whenever you like.

lines.name: Margaret
lines.text: Will I actually see the tooth?

lines.name: Mahesh
lines.text: Not the tooth itself. It's kept inside a golden casket. During the ceremony, the doors open and you can see the casket.

lines.name: Margaret
lines.text: When is the ceremony?

lines.name: Mahesh
lines.text: There's one this evening, with drums. It gets crowded, so I'd suggest standing at the side, where it's quieter.

lines.name: Margaret
lines.text: That sounds perfect for me. Do I need a ticket?

lines.name: Mahesh
lines.text: Yes. I'll buy it for you at the official ticket counter. Please keep it with you.

lines.name: Margaret
lines.text: Thank you, dear. You're very patient with an old lady.

lines.name: Mahesh
lines.text: It's my pleasure. Shall we sit on that bench for a minute before we go in?

lines.name: Margaret
lines.text: Yes, please. Then I'm ready.

scenarios.title: Which beach this month?
scenarios.segment: Beach safety and monsoon seasons on each coast
scenarios.setting: Guesthouse in Colombo, in June.
scenarios.characters: Host: Ravi, 35, guesthouse owner and keen swimmer. Tourist: Liam, 28, from Ireland, a beginner surfer.
scenarios.resolution: Liam switches from the rough south coast to Arugam Bay, which is in season, and knows the red-flag, rip-current and no-lifeguard rules.

notes.text: Explain the two monsoons as a simple swap: south and west rough in mid-year, east rough at the end of the year.
Safety advice works best as short commands: float, swim sideways, wave for help.
Never promise a beach is safe; say “usually calm” and “check the flags”.

sayThis.say: The sea is rough at this time of year
sayThis.not: Sea is very rough these days, no?

lines.name: Ravi
lines.text: Good morning, Liam. You said you want to go to the beach. Where are you thinking?

lines.name: Liam
lines.text: Mirissa or Unawatuna. My friends loved them.

lines.name: Ravi
lines.text: They're beautiful, but it's June. The sea is rough at this time of year on the south and west coasts. It's monsoon season there.

lines.name: Liam
lines.text: Really? It's sunny today in Colombo.

lines.name: Ravi
lines.text: It can be sunny, but the waves are big and the currents are strong. Many beaches have red flags up.

lines.name: Liam
lines.text: So where should we go?

lines.name: Ravi
lines.text: The east coast. From about May to September it's the dry season there. Arugam Bay is great for surfing, and Trincomalee is calm for swimming.

lines.name: Liam
lines.text: Arugam Bay sounds perfect. I surf a bit.

lines.name: Ravi
lines.text: Then you'll love it. And in December it's the other way round: the south is calm and the east is rainy.

lines.name: Liam
lines.text: Good to know for next time. Are there lifeguards?

lines.name: Ravi
lines.text: At some busy beaches, yes, but many beaches have none. Always ask locally, and swim where other people are swimming.

lines.name: Liam
lines.text: What about rip currents?

lines.name: Ravi
lines.text: If one pulls you out, don't swim against it. Float, swim sideways, parallel to the beach, and wave for help.

lines.name: Liam
lines.text: Okay. Anything else?

lines.name: Ravi
lines.text: Don't swim after drinking or at night. And respect the red flags, even if the water looks calm.

lines.name: Liam
lines.text: Got it. How do we get to Arugam Bay?

lines.name: Ravi
lines.text: It's a long drive, about seven or eight hours. You could stop in Ella for a night, then go down to the coast.

lines.name: Liam
lines.text: Ella, then the beach. That's a great plan!

lines.name: Ravi
lines.text: I'll help you find a driver. Enjoy the east coast.

scenarios.title: SIM cards, cash and cards on the first morning
scenarios.setting: Front desk of a hotel in Colombo, the morning after a late-night arrival.
scenarios.characters: Front office officer: Anusha, 25, front office officer. Tourist: Kenji Tanaka, 30, from Japan, on his first trip to South Asia, who arrived too late to buy a SIM at the airport.
scenarios.resolution: Kenji knows where to buy and register a SIM, takes rupees from the lobby ATM in local currency, and has clear rules on where cards and cash work and how to keep his card safe.

notes.text: Greet by name and link to what you know (“after your late arrival”); it shows you read the booking.
Don't quote prices that change; send the guest to the official price board. Explain the “pay in your own currency?” ATM question simply: choose rupees.
Offer a bridge until the problem is solved (the Wi-Fi password) and close with an open offer of more help.

sayThis.say: There's an ATM here in the lobby
sayThis.not: ATM is there in the lobby.

lines.name: Anusha
lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Tanaka, and welcome to Colombo. I hope you slept well after your late arrival.

lines.name: Kenji Tanaka
lines.text: Yes, thank you. I need a SIM card and some cash today. Where can I get them?

lines.name: Anusha
lines.text: There's a Dialog shop two minutes' walk from the hotel, and we have an ATM here in the lobby. Shall I show you on the map?

lines.name: Kenji Tanaka
lines.text: Yes, please. Which SIM is best?

lines.name: Anusha
lines.text: Dialog and Mobitel have good coverage almost everywhere, and Hutch is fine in the cities. You'll need your passport to register.

lines.name: Kenji Tanaka
lines.text: Passport, okay. How much is it?

lines.name: Anusha
lines.text: The shop shows its tourist packages on a board, with data and prices, so you can compare.

lines.name: Kenji Tanaka
lines.text: Good. Can I pay by card there?

lines.name: Anusha
lines.text: Usually, yes. But many small shops, tuk-tuks and buses take cash only, so please carry some rupees.

lines.name: Kenji Tanaka
lines.text: How much cash should I take?

lines.name: Anusha
lines.text: Enough for a few days of small things. Hotels and bigger restaurants take cards, and you can charge meals here to your room.

lines.name: Kenji Tanaka
lines.text: I'll try the lobby ATM now. Oh, it's asking if I want to pay in yen or in rupees.

lines.name: Anusha
lines.text: Please choose rupees. If you choose yen, the machine sets the exchange rate, and it's usually worse.

lines.name: Kenji Tanaka
lines.text: Rupees. Okay, done. Is it safe to use ATMs in town?

lines.name: Anusha
lines.text: Yes, but use ATMs inside banks or hotels if you can, and cover the keypad. And never give your card to anyone to take out money for you.

lines.name: Kenji Tanaka
lines.text: Someone would ask that?

lines.name: Anusha
lines.text: It's rare, but it has happened to tourists. Please keep your card with you at all times.

lines.name: Kenji Tanaka
lines.text: Thank you. That's very clear.

lines.name: Anusha
lines.text: You're welcome. Until your SIM works, the Wi-Fi password is on your key card. Please let me know if there's anything else I can do.

scenarios.title: An upset stomach and the pharmacy
scenarios.setting: Guesthouse in Ella, breakfast time.
scenarios.characters: Host: Nilmini, 49, runs the guesthouse with her husband. Tourist: Chloe, 23, from the UK, travelling alone.
scenarios.resolution: Chloe switches to safe water, gets rehydration salts from the pharmacy, and knows the warning signs that mean she should see a doctor.

notes.text: Ask simple yes/no health questions first (fever, blood, how long), then give advice.
Give the local product name (“Jeewanee”) so the tourist can ask for it.
Always give clear red flags for seeing a doctor; you are a host, not a doctor.

sayThis.say: Do you have a fever?
sayThis.not: Is there fever?

lines.name: Nilmini
lines.text: Good morning, Chloe. You didn't come for breakfast. Are you okay?

lines.name: Chloe
lines.text: Not really. My stomach's been bad since last night. I think it was something I ate.

lines.name: Nilmini
lines.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Do you have a fever?

lines.name: Chloe
lines.text: No fever, just cramps and diarrhoea.

lines.name: Nilmini
lines.text: Have you been drinking tap water?

lines.name: Chloe
lines.text: Only for brushing my teeth. And there was ice in my juice yesterday.

lines.name: Nilmini
lines.text: Ice can be a problem. Please use bottled or boiled water only, even for your teeth, until you feel better.

lines.name: Chloe
lines.text: Okay. Is there a pharmacy near here?

lines.name: Nilmini
lines.text: Yes, on the main road, five minutes' walk. Ask for oral rehydration salts. Here we call it “Jeewanee”. You mix it with clean water.

lines.name: Chloe
lines.text: Do I need a prescription?

lines.name: Nilmini
lines.text: Not for rehydration salts. The pharmacist speaks English and can suggest other medicine. Tell them about any allergies.

lines.name: Chloe
lines.text: Should I see a doctor?

lines.name: Nilmini
lines.text: If you get a fever, see blood, or you're not better in two days, yes. I can call a doctor or take you to the hospital.

lines.name: Chloe
lines.text: Thank you. I feel a bit embarrassed.

lines.name: Nilmini
lines.text: Please don't. It happens to lots of travellers. Rest today, and I'll make you some plain rice porridge.

lines.name: Chloe
lines.text: Is it spicy?

lines.name: Nilmini
lines.text: Not at all. It's soft rice cooked with a little coconut milk. It's what we give anyone with a bad stomach.

lines.name: Chloe
lines.text: That sounds perfect. And I'll skip the ice for now.

lines.name: Nilmini
lines.text: Good idea. I'll bring you a big bottle of water. Call me if you need anything.

scenarios.title: A ‘special festival’ and a gem shop
scenarios.setting: Pettah, Colombo, just before a walking tour.
scenarios.characters: Guide: Lahiru, 31, walking-tour guide. Tourist: Daniel, 34, from the USA, who has just been approached by a friendly stranger.
scenarios.resolution: Daniel recognises the trick, has a polite phrase to refuse touts, knows how to buy gems safely, and has the 1912 hotline.

notes.text: Protect the country's image: “most people are just being friendly” comes before the warning.
Describe the pattern (only today, government sale, ends at a shop), not the person.
Give the tourist a ready-made sentence to refuse politely.

sayThis.say: You don't have to buy anything
sayThis.not: No compulsory to buy.

lines.name: Lahiru
lines.text: Hi, Daniel. You look a bit confused. Is everything okay?

lines.name: Daniel
lines.text: I think so. A friendly man just told me there's a special elephant festival at a temple today, only today. He offered to take me in his tuk-tuk.

lines.name: Lahiru
lines.text: I see. Did he mention a gem shop or a government sale?

lines.name: Daniel
lines.text: Yes! He said there's a government gem sale that ends today. How did you know?

lines.name: Lahiru
lines.text: I've heard that story before. Most people who stop to chat are just being friendly, but this one is a common sales trick.

lines.name: Daniel
lines.text: So there's no festival?

lines.name: Lahiru
lines.text: Not today. Big festivals are announced well in advance, and there's no special government gem sale. Usually the trip ends at a shop, with a lot of pressure to buy.

lines.name: Daniel
lines.text: He seemed so nice.

lines.name: Lahiru
lines.text: He may be nice. He probably gets commission from the shop. It's not about Sri Lankans in general; it's one way a few people make money from visitors.

lines.name: Daniel
lines.text: What should I say if someone stops me again?

lines.name: Lahiru
lines.text: Smile and say, “No, thank you, I have plans.” Then keep walking. You don't need to explain.

lines.name: Daniel
lines.text: And if I really want to buy a sapphire?

lines.name: Lahiru
lines.text: Sri Lanka has beautiful gems. Go to a well-known shop, ask for a certificate and take your time. You don't have to buy anything.

lines.name: Daniel
lines.text: Is there a way to check if a gem is real?

lines.name: Lahiru
lines.text: Yes, the National Gem and Jewellery Authority can test gems. I can show you where its office is.

lines.name: Daniel
lines.text: That's really useful. I almost went with him.

lines.name: Lahiru
lines.text: You did the right thing by asking. And if anyone pressures you, call the tourist hotline on 1912.

lines.name: Daniel
lines.text: 1912. Got it. Thanks, Lahiru.

lines.name: Lahiru
lines.text: My pleasure. Now, shall we see a real temple? It's just around the corner.

scenarios.title: A lost phone, the front desk and the tourist police
scenarios.setting: Front desk of a hotel inside Galle Fort, late afternoon.
scenarios.characters: Front office officer: Chandima, 28, front office officer. Tourist: Olga Ivanova, 36, from Russia, who has just come back from the lighthouse without her phone.
scenarios.resolution: Olga's phone is called and the café checked, her account is locked, and she goes to the tourist police in a ride the hotel booked, with the right details and a request for a reference number for her insurer.

notes.text: Stay calm and give one step at a time: call, check nearby, lock, report.
Do what the hotel can do for the guest (call the phone, ring the café, book the ride, print the address) instead of only giving advice.
Tell the guest what to bring before they reach the police, and mention the insurance report; stressed guests often forget it.

sayThis.say: We need to make a police report
sayThis.not: We must put an entry at the police.

lines.name: Chandima
lines.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Ivanova. You look worried. Is everything all right?

lines.name: Olga Ivanova
lines.text: I can't find my phone. I had it at the lighthouse, and now it's gone. Maybe I left it on the wall.

lines.name: Chandima
lines.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Let's try calling it first. May I have your number? I'll ring it from the desk phone.

lines.name: Olga Ivanova
lines.text: Yes, here. Is it ringing?

lines.name: Chandima
lines.text: It's ringing, but nobody's answering. Let me also call the café by the lighthouse. Sometimes people hand things in there.

lines.name: Olga Ivanova
lines.text: Thank you. Did they find it?

lines.name: Chandima
lines.text: I'm afraid not. Then please lock the phone from your account and change your important passwords. You're welcome to use our lobby computer.

lines.name: Olga Ivanova
lines.text: Doing it now. What should I do next?

lines.name: Chandima
lines.text: We should make a report with the tourist police. They help visitors with this every day, and the officers speak English.

lines.name: Olga Ivanova
lines.text: What do I need to take?

lines.name: Chandima
lines.text: Your passport or a copy, the hotel address, and the phone's details: the make, the colour, and the IMEI number if you have it.

lines.name: Olga Ivanova
lines.text: The IMEI is on the box at home. My husband can send me a photo.

lines.name: Chandima
lines.text: Perfect. Please ask the officer for a copy of the report or a reference number. Your insurance company will want it.

lines.name: Olga Ivanova
lines.text: I didn't even think about insurance.

lines.name: Chandima
lines.text: Many people forget. I'll book a PickMe to the police station for you, and I'll print the hotel address for the report.

lines.name: Olga Ivanova
lines.text: Thank you. I was really panicking.

lines.name: Chandima
lines.text: That's completely understandable. If anyone hands the phone in, we'll call you on your husband's number. The tourist hotline, 1912, can also help.

lines.name: Olga Ivanova
lines.text: Thank you so much. You've been very kind.

lines.name: Chandima
lines.text: It's my pleasure, Mrs. Ivanova. Your ride is outside. Please let us know how it goes.

scenarios.title: Where should I go? A backpacker and a family
scenarios.setting: Common room of a hostel in Colombo, in November.
scenarios.characters: Host: Shehan, 29, hostel manager and former backpacker. Tourist: Zoe, 22, from New Zealand, travelling solo; her sister's family arrives in December.
scenarios.resolution: Zoe gets a budget hiking-and-beach route, and her sister gets a three-base family plan with a short elephant safari, all sent in writing.

notes.text: Ask before you recommend: interests, budget and who is travelling.
Give different advice to different travellers: hostels and hikes for backpackers; fewer moves and short activities for families.
Add one safety line to every recommendation (start early, a guide for Ella Rock, check the flags).

sayThis.say: It depends on what you enjoy
sayThis.not: All places are nice, you must go everywhere.

lines.name: Shehan
lines.text: So, Zoe, you have two weeks. What kind of trip do you want?

lines.name: Zoe
lines.text: Honestly, I don't know where to start. Everyone says something different.

lines.name: Shehan
lines.text: It depends on what you enjoy. Do you like hiking, beaches, history or wildlife?

lines.name: Zoe
lines.text: Hiking and beaches, mostly. And I'm on a budget.

lines.name: Shehan
lines.text: Then the hill country is perfect. Ella has easy hikes like Little Adam's Peak, and Ella Rock for a longer day.

lines.name: Zoe
lines.text: Is it safe to hike alone?

lines.name: Shehan
lines.text: The popular trails are busy, but start early and tell your guesthouse where you're going. For Ella Rock, a local guide is a good idea.

lines.name: Zoe
lines.text: Good tip. And beaches?

lines.name: Shehan
lines.text: In December the south coast is best: Mirissa, Hiriketiya, or Weligama if you want to learn to surf. The hostels there are great for meeting people.

lines.name: Zoe
lines.text: Sounds great. Actually, my sister is coming in December with her kids, aged four and seven. Where would you send them?

lines.name: Shehan
lines.text: For families, fewer hotel changes are better, because kids get tired. I'd suggest three bases: Kandy, the south coast and Udawalawe.

lines.name: Zoe
lines.text: Why Udawalawe?

lines.name: Shehan
lines.text: It's one of the best parks for seeing elephants, and a short safari is easier with small children. There's also the Elephant Transit Home, where orphaned calves are fed.

lines.name: Zoe
lines.text: The kids would love that. Are any beaches safe for small children?

lines.name: Shehan
lines.text: Unawatuna is usually calmer in December, but always check the flags and keep an eye on the kids.

lines.name: Zoe
lines.text: Thanks! Can you write this down for me?

lines.name: Shehan
lines.text: Of course. I'll send you a list on WhatsApp, with travel times between each place.

lines.name: Zoe
lines.text: You're a star, Shehan.

lines.name: Shehan
lines.text: Happy to help. Come back and tell me about Ella Rock!

scenarios.title: Planning for the Esala Perahera and Avurudu
scenarios.setting: Lakeside in Kandy at the end of a city tour, in October.
scenarios.characters: Guide: Dilan, 42, Kandy-based guide. Tourist: Fiona, 47, from the UK, travelling with her husband, who dislikes crowds.
scenarios.resolution: Fiona understands how the Perahera dates are set, how to watch it comfortably with a booked seat, the etiquette, and what Avurudu offers in April.

notes.text: Explain why dates move (the full moon) so tourists check each year instead of trusting an old blog.
Offer a follow-up (“I'll message you”); it creates a returning customer.
Mention the practical side of festivals: full hotels, closed shops, crowds.

sayThis.say: The dates change every year
sayThis.not: The dates are changing every year.

lines.name: Dilan
lines.text: You were asking about festivals. Have you heard of the Esala Perahera?

lines.name: Fiona
lines.text: The one with the elephants here in Kandy? We'd love to come back for it next year.

lines.name: Dilan
lines.text: That's the one. It's about ten nights of processions, with drummers, dancers, fire-twirlers and decorated elephants. It honours the Sacred Tooth Relic.

lines.name: Fiona
lines.text: When is it?

lines.name: Dilan
lines.text: Usually in July or August. The dates change every year, because they follow the full moon of the month of Esala. This year it was from 18 to 28 August.

lines.name: Fiona
lines.text: How will we know next year's dates?

lines.name: Dilan
lines.text: The Temple of the Tooth announces them. I'll message you as soon as they're out, so you can book a hotel early. Kandy gets very full.

lines.name: Fiona
lines.text: Where's the best place to watch?

lines.name: Dilan
lines.text: Many people book a seat along the route. The last nights are the biggest, but also the most crowded.

lines.name: Fiona
lines.text: My husband isn't good in big crowds. Will he be okay?

lines.name: Dilan
lines.text: A booked seat is much better than standing. Bring water, and be ready to sit for a few hours.

lines.name: Fiona
lines.text: Are there any rules we should know?

lines.name: Dilan
lines.text: It's a religious procession, so dress modestly and be quiet when the relic casket passes. Please don't use flash near the elephants.

lines.name: Fiona
lines.text: Got it. Are there other festivals we should know about?

lines.name: Dilan
lines.text: If you come in April, there's the Sinhala and Tamil New Year, Avurudu, in mid-April. Families make milk rice, play games and visit relatives.

lines.name: Fiona
lines.text: Can tourists join in?

lines.name: Dilan
lines.text: Yes! Many villages and hotels hold Avurudu games, and visitors are welcome. But many shops close for a few days, so book your transport early.

lines.name: Fiona
lines.text: August for the Perahera, April for New Year. We'll have to come twice!

lines.name: Dilan
lines.text: That's the best idea I've heard today.
